content: Liver flukes are parasitic organisms that can infect humans, leading to diseases of the liver and bile ducts. There are two primary families of liver flukes that cause human disease: the Opisthorchiidae family, which includes species such as Clonorchis and Opisthorchis, and the Fasciolidae family, which includes species such as Fasciola. These two families differ in their geographic distribution, life cycles, and the long-term outcomes of clinical infections. Clonorchiasis (Clonorchis Infection) Clonorchis is a type of liver fluke that can infect the liver, gallbladder, and bile ducts. This parasite, also referred to as the Chinese liver fluke, belongs to the Opisthorchiidae family. It is important to note that Clonorchis cannot be transmitted from one person to another, nor can it be contracted by drinking untreated water. Infections caused by Clonorchis can persist for several years, corresponding to the lifespan of the parasite. Fascioliasis (Fasciola Infection) Fasciola is another type of liver fluke that can infect the liver and bile ducts of humans and various animals, including sheep, cattle, goats, and other herbivorous domestic and wild animals. This parasite causes a disease known as fascioliasis, which is more commonly observed in individuals who live or work in close proximity to livestock in regions where animal infections are prevalent. Two species of Fasciola are known to infect humans: Fasciola hepatica: This is the primary species that infects humans and is also known as the common liver fluke or the sheep liver fluke. Fasciola gigantica: This related species primarily infects domestic and wild animals but can also infect humans. Fascioliasis has been reported on every continent except Antarctica and occurs in over 70 countries, particularly in areas with sheep, cattle, or goats. Humans typically acquire Fasciola infections by consuming raw watercress or other freshwater plants contaminated with the parasite's larvae. Infection can also occur by drinking contaminated water or eating vegetables that have been washed or irrigated with such water. However, Fasciola cannot be transmitted from one person to another. Opisthorchiasis (Opisthorchis Infection) Opisthorchis is a liver fluke that can infect the liver, gallbladder, and bile ducts. This parasite belongs to the Opisthorchiidae family and includes species such as Opisthorchis viverrini (commonly known as the Southeast Asian liver fluke) and Opisthorchis felineus (commonly known as the cat liver fluke). Similar to Clonorchis, Opisthorchis cannot be transmitted from one person to another, nor can it be contracted by drinking untreated water. Infections caused by Opisthorchis can also persist for several years, corresponding to the lifespan of the parasite.
